View of a man standing on a bridge over a river between Jowai and Jarain, possibly the one described by Hutton as follows: 'near Maput village [now Mupyut or Mawpyut], we came to a fine megalithic bridge made of old by the Jaintia princes. It is called Thluumwi [now Thlu Amwi/Thlu Muwi] which I understand refers to the fact that there are three stone spans, but as a matter of fact there are six, spanning 96 feet from end to end, though three are larger than the others, or rather were, for one, alas, is broken and fallen into the bed of the stream, its place being taken by a modern span of wood and corrugated iron.' (tour diary, 20 October 1925)

View along a bridge to two turbaned men standing and sitting on steps down to the bridge, probably the one described by Hutton as follows: 'Between Jarain and Syndai the Um-niakaneh river is crossed by a much finer megalithic bridge . . . it has lost one span. Originally it was either completed or planned to consist of three gothic arches built with enormous blocks of stone, but only one such arch remains and the others either collapsed in construction or afterwards and are now spanned by huge flat slabs, the footway being carried down to the flat slabs by steps from the arch top.' (tour diary, 21 October 1925)

View from the river bank, at middle distance, of a bridge over a rocky river, possibly the one the one across the Um-niakaneh river described by Hutton on 21 October 1925, but possibly the one he described on the next day: 'The Am-lubon river is crossed by a modern timber bridge resting on the piers of the megalithic one which preceded it.' (tour diary, 22 October 1925)

View of a pool with stone walls, probably the one between Syndai and Jaintiapur (now Jaintapur) described by Hutton as follows: 'A little further on is a tank cut entirely out of solid rock with gutter and drains likewise excavated out of the rock to bring the rain water from the slope above it to keep it full. The tank is 22'11" broad by 29'2" long round the edge and descends inside in three broad steps, the depth in the centre being 6' from the bottom to the level of the outer edge.' (tour diary, 22 October 1925)
Panoramic view of a large gathering of people at the market of Shillong, among long buildings with pointed towers, and on adjacent slopes, with horses and other domesticated animals.

View from the riverbank below of a turbaned man standing on a stone bridge, probably the one described by Hutton as follows: 'Between Jarain and Syndai the Um-niakaneh river is crossed by a much finer megalithic bridge . . . it has lost one span. Originally it was either completed or planned to consist of three gothic arches built with enormous blocks of stone, but only one such arch remains and the others either collapsed in construction or afterwards and are now spanned by huge flat slabs, the footway being carried down to the flat slabs by steps from the arch top.' (tour diary, 21 October 1925)

View of a stone carving, probably the one described by Hutton as follows: 'Between Jarain and Syndai the Um-niakaneh river is crossed by a much finer megalithic bridge . . . The outer pier of the arch was adorned, in what was, or would have been, the angle between the two arches, with a carved rosette of concentric circles and above that appeared a carving of a very horsey-looking lion with a waspish waist prancing in the boughs of a highly conventionalised pine tree. It must be inferred from its tail that it was a lion, and it had a general family likeness to the lions on the Kasomari monoliths and on the Manipur stone.' (tour diary, 21 October 1925)
